question: What primary role does the nurse fulfill during the medication administration process?

options.A: The primary author of pharmacological treatment plans
options.B: The sole financial auditor for hospital drug inventories
options.C: The manufacturer of clinical pharmaceutical compounds
options.D: The final safety barrier protecting the patient from harm

explanation: The nurse acts as the last line of defense, catching potential prescription or dispensing errors before a drug reaches the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is medication administration considered a high-risk nursing responsibility?

options.A: Because patients rarely cooperate with oral medication schedules
options.B: Because nurses are legally liable for manufacturing errors made in pharmacies
options.C: Because it is the most time-consuming task on any hospital shift
options.D: Because every dose carries both therapeutic benefits and inherent risks of adverse effects

explanation: Drugs are powerful chemical agents that can heal or harm, requiring careful monitoring for unintended negative reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h1)

question: How many times should a nurse compare the medication label against the prescription order?

options.A: Four times to be completely safe

explanation: Checking the drug against the order upon retrieval, during preparation, and at the bedside catches discrepancies early. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h2)

question: A nurse is about to give an oral antibiotic to a patient asleep in bed. What is the correct initial action regarding patient identification?

options.A: Check the chart hanging at the foot of the bed and proceed quietly
options.B: Assume the identity is correct because the bed assignment has not changed
options.C: Check the identification wristband and ask the patient to state their name
options.D: Ask the neighboring patient in the ward to confirm who is sleeping in the bed

explanation: Using two unique identifiers protects against administration errors, especially if patients have been moved between beds. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h2)

question: Why must a nurse check vital signs before administering certain cardiovascular medications?

options.A: To satisfy routine administrative paperwork requirements
options.B: To determine if the patient has any active skin infections
options.C: To prevent adverse events like severe hypotension or dangerous bradycardia
options.D: To calculate the exact financial cost of the hospital stay

explanation: Drugs that alter heart rate or blood pressure require baseline measurements to ensure safe administration thresholds are met. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which assessment is absolutely mandatory before administering any prescribed medication?
explanation: Reviewing allergy history prevents acute hypersensitivity reactions and life-threatening anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h3)

question: What happens if a nurse crushes an enteric-coated tablet before administration?

options.A: The specialized delivery mechanism is ruined, causing a dangerous rapid drug release
options.B: The drug dissolves safely in the stomach instead of the intestines
options.C: The medication becomes completely inactive and useless
options.D: The taste improves significantly for pediatric patients

explanation: Enteric coatings protect the stomach lining or delay drug absorption; breaking them alters pharmacokinetics dangerously. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following actions is NOT permitted when handling multi-dose medication vials?

options.A: Storing the vial according to the manufacturer temperature guidelines
options.B: Failing to record the date and time when the vial is first opened
options.C: Checking the expiration date printed on the packaging label
options.D: Cleaning the rubber stopper with an alcohol swab before piercing

explanation: Multi-dose vials carry contamination risks and must always be dated upon opening to ensure they are discarded safely. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which drug administration route provides the fastest systemic onset of action?
explanation: Injecting medication directly into the bloodstream bypasses absorption barriers, achieving immediate peak concentration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why are sublingual medications absorbed much faster than swallowed oral tablets?

options.A: Gastric acid breaks down sublingual pills instantly upon contact
options.B: Saliva neutralizes the chemical structure of the drug to speed up transit
options.C: The patient swallows the drug faster when it is placed under the tongue
options.D: Rich blood supply under the tongue allows direct entry into circulation, avoiding first-pass metabolism

explanation: The sublingual mucosa contains a dense capillary network that absorbs drugs straight into systemic veins, bypassing the liver. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why is charting a medication before actually administering it considered a dangerous practice?

options.A: It causes the pharmacy inventory system to order extra stock automatically
options.B: It violates the patient's right to financial transparency
options.C: It creates a false record if an interruption prevents the dose from being given
options.D: It slows down the speed of intravenous drug infusion pumps

explanation: If a nurse documents administration beforehand and gets distracted, another nurse might accidentally administer a double dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the legal status of a medication that was given to a patient but never documented in the chart?

options.B: Automatically documented by hospital electronic systems
options.D: Considered acceptable if the patient verbalized recovery

explanation: Courts and regulatory bodies operate on the principle that if it is not documented, it was not done. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h6)

question: A nurse realizes they have just administered the wrong medication dose to a patient. What is the immediate priority action?

options.A: Blame the pharmacy department in the formal incident report
options.B: Wait until the end of the shift to see if symptoms develop
options.C: Hide the medication packaging in the utility room waste bin
options.D: Assess the patient's clinical condition and notify the physician

explanation: Patient safety and immediate clinical stabilization always take precedence over administrative paperwork when an error occurs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a non-punitive incident reporting culture in healthcare?

options.A: To uncover system weaknesses and prevent the recurrence of mistakes
options.B: To satisfy international tourism accreditation standards
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing replacement drugs
options.D: To ensure that negligent nurses are fired immediately without hearings

explanation: Blame-free reporting encourages staff to speak up about safety flaws, allowing organizations to fix underlying systemic vulnerabilities. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h7)
